name: Harpeth River State Park
unique: A string of river access sites along the Harpeth including the Narrows, where a tunnel was cut through a ridge by enslaved laborers around 1818 to run water to an iron mill, leaving a bluff trail and a rock arch over the river.
buzz: The tunnel and the overlook are the photograph everyone takes, and it is a fifteen minute walk from the lot. Paddlers float the Harpeth below it in summer.

name: Mound Bottom
unique: A Mississippian era mound complex of more than a hundred acres in a bend of the Harpeth, occupied from roughly 900 to 1300, reachable only on ranger led hikes because the site is unexcavated and unprotected by fences.
buzz: The guided walk is the only way in and it books out. Standing on a platform mound above the river with nobody else around is the reason people go.

name: Cheatham Lake
unique: The Cumberland River impounded behind Cheatham Lock and Dam, with Corps campgrounds, a tailwater trout fishery below the dam and quiet water above it twenty minutes from Nashville.
buzz: The tailwater below the dam is the local trout secret and the lake itself is where everybody takes a boat on a summer evening.

name: Ashland City Courthouse Square
unique: A small courthouse square above the Cumberland in a county that stayed rural while Nashville grew around it, with a diner, a hardware store and a river overlook.
buzz: Twenty five minutes from downtown Nashville and a different century. The river view from the bluff is the best free thing in the county.

name: Montgomery Bell State Park
unique: Nearly four thousand acres of reclaimed iron works land with three lakes, a hotel and conference center, a golf course, and a replica log cabin marking where the Cumberland Presbyterian Church was organized in 1810.
buzz: The lakes and trails are quietly excellent and the inn makes it a cheap weekend. The iron furnace ruins in the woods are the part history people come for.

name: Old Spencer Mill
unique: A water powered grist mill and miller's house on Spencer Mill Road, restored and run by a preservation group that fires it up for demonstrations and corn grinding.
buzz: When the wheel is turning it is worth the drive on its own. Otherwise it is a photogenic piece of 1800s industry in a hollow, which is still worth the stop.

name: Cumberland Furnace
unique: One of the oldest iron making communities in Tennessee, with the furnace stack, company store building and workers' houses still standing along the road where ore was smelted from the 1790s into the twentieth century.
buzz: No visitor center, no admission, just a village that exists because of iron. The surviving furnace and store are the reason to slow down.

name: Loretta Lynn Ranch
unique: Loretta Lynn's own ranch at Hurricane Mills, with a museum of stage clothes and cars, a replica of her childhood home, a campground and a motocross track that hosts amateur nationals.
buzz: The museum is a fan pilgrimage and the motocross weekends fill the county. The mill and the old town buildings on the property are the part non fans enjoy.

name: Johnsonville State Historic Park
unique: Thirteen hundred acres on the Tennessee River bluff where a Union supply depot was burned in 1864, with earthworks, a cemetery, the old railroad cut and trails along the water.
buzz: The railroad cut dug by hand through the ridge and the bluff over the river are the highlights. Almost empty on weekdays.

name: St. Patrick's Irish Picnic
customer: Barbecue people, families, church picnic regulars
unique: The 172nd edition of a church barbecue in McEwen where meat is cooked over permanent pits dug into the ground, served with live music, games and a homecoming that brings families back from out of state.
buzz: People plan summer around it. The barbecue is the point, the lines are long and the whole thing is run by volunteers.

name: Duck River
unique: A river that conservation groups call one of the most biologically diverse in North America, with more than fifty freshwater mussel species, floatable through Humphreys County over gravel bars and riffles.
buzz: Paddlers love the current and the lack of development. Biologists come from other states to look at mussels and darters in a river most people float without knowing.

name: Wells Creek Basin
customer: Geology people, science teachers, road trippers
unique: A two mile wide circular valley in Houston and Stewart counties that is the eroded root of a meteorite impact crater, its rock shattered and folded in patterns you can see from the road and the ridges above it.
buzz: It is one of the few impact craters in the eastern United States you can drive through, and there is no sign telling you so. Geology field trips from three states come here.

name: Erin Irish Day Celebration
customer: Families, parade people, Irish heritage travellers
unique: A one day Irish festival in a Tennessee town that leans into the name, with a parade, music, food and a chunk of stone on the courthouse lawn that locals kiss for luck.
buzz: Small town parade with a big crowd. The Blarney Stone on the square is the photo everybody takes.

name: Erin Historic District
unique: A downtown of brick storefronts and a courthouse square on the old stage road between Nashville and the Tennessee River, with the historic district covering the commercial block and the houses around it.
buzz: Quiet, cheap and unmodernized. Pair it with the crater and the iron furnace for a full afternoon.

name: Bear Springs Iron Furnace
unique: The stone remains of a nineteenth century iron furnace in the woods near Erin, one of several that smelted local ore before the Civil War, with the slag heap and foundation still visible.
buzz: Overgrown, unsigned and genuinely atmospheric. Bring boots and expect to hunt for it.

name: Fort Donelson National Battlefield
customer: Civil War people, families, history travellers
unique: The Confederate river fort that Grant took in February 1862, opening the Cumberland and the South to Union gunboats, with reconstructed earthworks, river batteries above the water and a national cemetery.
buzz: The river battery walk and the earthworks are the best preserved parts, and the rangers explain why this surrender mattered more than most battles. Free, and rarely crowded.

name: Land Between the Lakes
unique: A 170,000 acre national recreation area between Kentucky Lake and Lake Barkley with a drive through elk and bison prairie, a planetarium, a working 1850s farm and hundreds of miles of trail.
buzz: The elk and bison prairie is the thing kids remember. The farm and the planetarium make it a full day, and the woods are empty compared to a national park.

name: Cross Creeks National Wildlife Refuge
dates: Year round, best November to February
unique: Almost nine thousand acres of river bottoms and bluffs on the Cumberland where waterfowl winter by the thousand, with a driving tour and blinds that are drawn by permit.
buzz: In January the Canada geese and ducks are thick enough to hear before you see them. Birders rate it as one of the better winter spots in middle Tennessee.

name: Dover Hotel
unique: The two story tavern where Confederate general Simon Bolivar Buckner surrendered his army to Grant in February 1862, still standing on the Dover street where it happened.
buzz: A small building with one large event attached to it. The park service opens it seasonally and the ranger talk is worth timing a visit for.

name: Kentucky Lake on the Stewart County Shore
company: US Army Corps of Engineers / Tennessee Valley Authority
unique: The eastern shore of a 160,000 acre reservoir with bays, Corps campgrounds and a crappie and bass fishery that supports a whole tourist economy in Dover.
buzz: Spring crappie fishing is the local calendar. The lake is big enough that you can find a quiet bay on a holiday weekend.
